scenes.title: The Binomial Theorem
scenes.promise: Expand any power of a bracket — and pick out one term without expanding at all.
scenes.narration: Welcome to the Binomial Theorem. By the end of this, you'll be able to expand any power of a bracket — and pick out a single term without expanding anything at all.

scenes.heading: Why expanding by hand dies
scenes.text:
Expanding $(1+x)^2$ by hand is fine. $(1+x)^3$ — still fine.

By $(1+x)^5$ you are multiplying five brackets and collecting six terms. One slip anywhere wrecks the lot.

This topic gives you a formula that writes any of these down in one line — and grabs any single term on its own.
scenes.narration: Expanding one plus x, all squared, by hand is fine. Cubed — still fine. But by the power of five you're multiplying five brackets and collecting six terms, and one slip anywhere wrecks the lot. This topic gives you a formula that writes any of these down in one line — and grabs any single term on its own.

scenes.heading: The same curve, one power higher each time
scenes.caption: Each power of $(1+x)$ is still just a polynomial. Watch the coefficients: $1,1$ → $1,2,1$ → $1,3,3,1$ → $1,4,6,4,1$ — each row is the previous row's neighbours added together (Pascal's triangle).
narration: Every power of one plus x is still just a polynomial. Start with the power one: that's one plus x, a straight line. Watch the coefficients — one, one.
Square it, and you get one plus two x plus x squared. The coefficients: one, two, one.
Now the cube. You get one plus three x, plus three x squared, plus x cubed. The coefficients: one, three, three, one.
Power four: one, four, six, four, one. Each row is the previous row's neighbours added together — that's Pascal's triangle.

scenes.heading: The numbers in front
scenes.text:
Those coefficients — $1, 4, 6, 4, 1$ — are the **binomial coefficients**, written $\binom{n}{r}$ and read "$n$ choose $r$".

You never work them out by hand: press $^nC_r$ on your calculator. $\binom{7}{2}$ is 7 $\,^nC_r\,$ 2 $\,= 21$.
scenes.narration: Those coefficients — one, four, six, four, one — are called the binomial coefficients. We write them as n choose r. You never work them out by hand: press the n C r button on your calculator. Seven choose two is seven, n C r, two — and that gives twenty-one.

scenes.heading: The binomial theorem — it's on your formula sheet

callouts.label: $a$'s power falls, $b$'s rises — in every term the two powers add to $n$

narration: Here's the binomial theorem — the whole expansion, written once. And yes, it's on your formula sheet.
It starts at a to the power n. All a, no b.
Then, term by term, a's power falls and b's power rises. In every single term, the two powers add up to n.
And it ends at b to the power n. Count them — there are n plus one terms in all.

scenes.heading: The workhorse: the general term
scenes.intro: One formula grabs any term on its own — also on the formula sheet:

callouts.label: the $(r+1)$th term — $r=3$ gives the 4th term, not the 3rd
second term's power rises: $r$ — its sign stays inside

narration: Now the workhorse: the general term. One formula grabs any term on its own, and it's on the formula sheet too. T, r plus one, equals n choose r, times a to the power n minus r, times b to the power r.
First, the name. T with subscript r plus one is the term in position r plus one. So r equals three gives you the fourth term, not the third. That one catches people out.
n choose r is the coefficient. Press n C r on your calculator.
The first term's power falls — it's n minus r.
The second term's power rises — it's r. And whatever sign b carries stays inside that power.

scenes.heading: Watch it work

steps.note: Match the formula: $a=2$, $b=3x$, $n=5$. The whole of $3x$ is $b$ — the 3 rides inside the power.
The $x$'s only come from $(3x)^r$, so the power of $x$ is $r$.
Substitute $r=3$ everywhere — and $T_{3+1}$ is the 4th term.
Coefficient of $x^3$: $\,1080$. No full expansion anywhere.

narration: Let's watch it work. Find the coefficient of x cubed in two plus three x, all to the power five. Match it to the formula: a is two, b is three x, and n is five. The whole of three x is b — the three rides inside the power.
We want x cubed. The x's only come from three x to the power r, so the power of x is r. That means r equals three.
Now substitute r equals three everywhere. Five choose three, times two to the power two, times three x, all cubed. And remember: T three plus one is the fourth term.
Five choose three is ten, from the calculator. Two squared is four. And three x, all cubed, is twenty-seven x cubed.
Multiply through: one thousand and eighty x cubed. So the coefficient of x cubed is one thousand and eighty — and we never expanded a thing.

scenes.heading: When a bracket sits in front
scenes.text:
Exams love $(k+2x)(\ldots)^6$. Don't expand everything.

Each part of the front bracket picks out whichever term of the expansion lands on the power you want. Want $x^3$ overall? Then $k$ needs the bracket's $x^3$ term, and $2x$ needs the bracket's $x^2$ term.

Expand only as far as you need — then collect.
scenes.narration: Exams love a bracket sitting in front — something like k plus two x, times another bracket to the power six. Don't expand everything. Each part of the front bracket picks out whichever term of the expansion lands on the power you want. Want x cubed overall? Then k needs the bracket's x cubed term, and two x needs the bracket's x squared term. Expand only as far as you need — then collect.

scenes.prompt: Your turn — a real O-Level question (GCE 2023). Use the general term on the bracket, then pair each part of $(k+2x)$ with the right term.
scenes.why: $k$ pairs with the bracket's $x^3$ term and $2x$ pairs with its $x^2$ term: $-20k + 2(60) = 0$, so $k = 6$.
scenes.narration: Your turn — a real O-Level question, from the 2023 GCE paper. Pause here and work it out. Use the general term on the bracket, then pair each part of k plus two x with the right term. Type your value of k when you're ready.

scenes.heading: The other classic: the term independent of x
scenes.intro: "Independent of $x$" means the power of $x$ is ZERO. Find that term in $\left(x^2 + \frac{2}{x}\right)^{\!6}$.

steps.note: The habit that earns the marks: (numbers) × (powers of $x$). $\frac{1}{x^r} = x^{-r}$.
Multiplying powers of $x$: ADD the exponents. $12 - 2r - r = 12 - 3r$.
Set the power to zero and solve. $r$ must land on a whole number — if it doesn't, the term does not exist.

narration: The other classic: the term independent of x. Independent of x means the power of x is zero. Let's find that term in x squared plus two over x, all to the power six. Same workhorse: a is x squared, b is two over x, and n is six.

Now the habit that earns the marks: numbers on one side, powers of x on the other. Six choose r, times two to the power r — that's the number part. Then x to the power twelve minus two r, times x to the power minus r — because one over x to the r is x to the minus r.
Multiplying powers of x means adding the exponents. Twelve minus two r, minus r, gives twelve minus three r.
Set that power to zero and solve: twelve minus three r equals zero, so r equals four. r must land on a whole number — if it doesn't, the term simply doesn't exist.
Substitute back. T five equals six choose four, times two to the power four. That's fifteen times sixteen — two hundred and forty. There's your term independent of x.

scenes.heading: The slip that costs the most marks
scenes.text:
When the bracket is $(a-bx)^n$, the minus lives INSIDE $b$.

$(-2x)^3 = -8x^3$ — the power hits the coefficient AND the sign AND the $x$. Odd $r$ keeps the minus; even $r$ kills it.

Write the second term in brackets, with its sign, every single time.
scenes.narration: Here's the slip that costs the most marks. When the bracket is a minus b x, all to the power n, the minus lives inside b. Minus two x, all cubed, is minus eight x cubed — the power hits the coefficient, the sign, and the x. Odd r keeps the minus; even r kills it. So write the second term in brackets, with its sign, every single time.

scenes.prompt: Last one. "No term in $x^2$" means that coefficient equals zero — and keep the minus inside $\left(-\frac{a}{3}x\right)^{\!r}$ while you work.
scenes.why: Pairing up for $x^2$: $\;3 \times \frac{80a^2}{3} + 5 \times (-64a) = 80a^2 - 320a = 0$, so the positive constant is $a = 4$.
scenes.narration: Last one — your turn again. No term in x squared means that coefficient equals zero. Keep the minus inside the bracket while you work. Pause here, work it through, and type your value of a when you're ready.

scenes.heading: You own the workhorse now
scenes.text:
General term → one power of $x$ → set the power to what you want → solve for $r$ → substitute back.

That is the whole topic. Every exam variation is this loop with different scenery — go make it automatic.
scenes.narration: You own the workhorse now. General term, one power of x, set the power to what you want, solve for r, substitute back. That's the whole topic. Every exam variation is this same loop with different scenery — go and make it automatic.
